001_AN_F314.pdf.topics:
This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems, and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.

Following are the scope and objective of this course: a. Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion. b. Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures, propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions. c. Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems. d. Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering.

002_BIO_F101.pdf.topics:
Properties of living systems, Biological macromolecules, Basic physiological processes, Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant tissues and Cell cycle analysis.

The course is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies to solve some of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of practical biology.

005_BIO_F213.pdf.topics: A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure, intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental biology.

007_BIO_F311.pdf.topics:
The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation. Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.

Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology.

Emphasis will be given to understand the plant tissue systems, water and mineral nutrient uptake and their distribution, mechanism of transpiration and photosynthate transport, the role of hormones in plant growth & developmental and mechanism of flowering.

Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding, Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice models, usage of modeling packages.

The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and structural biology. It describes the functionality, advantages, and limitations of standard computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data in a research or industry laboratory environment.

021_BIO_G532.pdf.topics:
Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations. Biomodeling is designed to provide students the first-hand experience of modelling biomolecules to elucidate the relationships between sequence, structure and function. Specifically, different computing strategies for the simulation of biomolecules will be discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.

The student would learn how to collect data suitable for statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of significance.

Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology and will create research interest among the students.

027_BIOT_F424.pdf.topics:
The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course, a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food Biotechnology will be discussed.

The aim of this course is providing the students with basic knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors. These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

037_BITS_F214.pdf.topics: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures, economic systems, and global governance. The course begins with an introduction to foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a basic orientation to how technologies are developed and adopted. Overall, it critically assesses the societal responsibilities and consequences of scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.

040_BITS_F225.pdf.topics:
Environment, human population, and industrialization; natural resources and the impact of man-made activities on them; structure and function of ecosystem, population ecology, biodiversity and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact assessment.

The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India. The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment, different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other electives/projects in these areas.

A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera- tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks, queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute- force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in- cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis. Objectives • Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob- lems. • Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority queues) for complex applications. • Usealgorithmictechniques(brute-force,greedy,divide-and-conquer,dynamicprogramming) to address real-world challenges. • Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.

043_BITS_F314.pdf.topics:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.

Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.

044_BITS_F327.pdf.topics:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.

This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles. Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing intelligent robotic systems. CO2 Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation. CO3 Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators. CO4 Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for autonomous robotic manipulation. _

049_BITS_F416.pdf.topics:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.

051_BITS_F429.pdf.course_title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment
051_BITS_F429.pdf.makeup_policy: Make-up will be granted for genuine cases only.
051_BITS_F429.pdf.topics:
This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells, fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation, nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment, and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.

Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3 modules as decribed below. o Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology o Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector o Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector. The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).

This course is an introduction to the basic theory and practice of cryptographic techniques used in information security. The course is intended to understand the mathematical concepts used for designing cryptosystems. The focus would be on the mathematical concepts from Number Theory and Abstract Algebra. We will delve into topics such as encryption (private-key and public-key), digital signatures, user authentication, key management, cryptographic hashing, Network security protocols, public-key infrastructure, digital rights management, and advancement in modern cryptology such as Identity Based Encryption, Steganography and Watermarking, Post-Quantum Cryptography, and Zero- Knowledge protocols. Prerequisites: The course is self-contained, however a basic understanding of probability theory, complexity theory, and modular arithmetic from number theory would be helpful. The course is intended for advanced undergraduates and master students. Course Objectives: Lectures deal with mathematical cryptography and related mathematical concepts required for modern cryptography and information security. The objective is to discuss and learn about basic tools and applications used in modern cryptography and to learn about some cryptographic protocols. On successful completion of the course students should be able to: understand basic principles and results of the theory of secure communication; know principles and problems of basic cryptosystems for encryption (both private and public key), digital signing and authentication; know methods to create core cryptographic protocols primitives; analyze and practically use simple cryptosystems; be understand basic principles of post-quantum cryptography and steganography. _

059_BITS_F468.pdf.topics:
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.

NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?

076_CE_F213.pdf.topics: The compulsory disciplinary course has been designed to introduce the basic concepts of geodesy (surveying) for Civil Engineering students. Different basic and advanced methods of measurements and traversing have been included so that the student will be able to handle a given project independently, irrespective of whether it is a road or any other infrastructure project. Important issues like curve setting, calculation of areas and volumes, which form part and parcel of any field civil engineer in his/her day-to-day activity. Hence, in this course, these areas have also been included. Scope & Objective: The course introduces the students to various basic techniques in surveying, viz., chain, compass, theodolite, plane table, tacheometry, traversing, and calculation of areas and volumes, along with fundamentals of a few advanced surveying techniques. Course Learning Outcomes: After successful completion of this course, students will be able to: ▪ Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of surveying, including methods of linear measurements and handling common field equipment such as chains, tapes, and compasses. ▪ Execute and analyze compass traversing, including the computation and correction of bearings, and apply techniques for accurate plotting and area determination. ▪ Perform differential and profile levelling and interpret level books for reduced level determination, accounting for curvature and refraction. ▪ Conduct contouring operations and generate contour maps using field measurements and appropriate plotting techniques. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division ▪ Carry out plane table and tacheometric surveys and apply relevant graphical and mathematical methods for plotting and distance/elevation computations. ▪ Design and set out simple and transition curves for civil infrastructure projects using chain, tape, and theodolite methods. ▪ Compute areas and volumes from cross-sections and contour maps and interpret mass haul diagrams relevant to earthworks. ▪ Demonstrate knowledge of modern surveying technologies, including total stations, photogrammetry, and remote sensing, and their practical applications. ▪ Analyze sources of error in surveying measurements and apply appropriate corrections to enhance the accuracy and reliability of data. ▪ Apply theoretical knowledge in field conditions by conducting various practical exercises such as chain surveying, curve setting, and use of total stations and GIS software. 078_CE_F231.pdf.topics:
Fluid Mechanics is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics, especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics, buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and similitude. The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.

• Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications • Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques • Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces • Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies • Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow, control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions • Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems • Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches • Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction • Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles • Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude

General requirement for satisfactory performance of shallow foundations, general, local and punching shear failures, bearing capacity, settlement, tilt and rotation of foundations, proportioning of Shallow Foundations, footings on layered soils and slopes, Deep foundations, capacity of single and group Piles, laterally loaded pile, Earth Pressure theories, Retaining structures, design and checks for stability, Stability of slopes, Introduction to Ground Improvement Techniques and geosynthetics with applications, Introduction to machine foundations for different type of machines, Introduction to geotechnical earthquake engineering and liquefaction of soils, computer applications in foundation design

Analysis of foundations and retaining structures (Shallow foundations, pile foundations, machine foundations, retaining walls, slope stability etc.) considering all geotechnical aspects. 081_CE_F320.pdf.topics:
Design Philosophies: Introduction to working stress design philosophy; Limit State design philosophy, Limit State design of Singly reinforced and doubly reinforced rectangular and flanged section beams; Design of one-way and two-way slabs in flexure; Design of beams and slabs for shear; Design of beams and slabs for bond, anchorage and development length; Design of beams and slabs for serviceability; Limit state design of columns subjected to axial load, and axial load plus uni-axial and bi-axial bending; Design of footings under the columns; Design of simple staircases.

In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently, the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond, and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.

082_CE_F331.pdf.topics: In-situ Testing Methods in Geotechnical Engineering is an introductory course to various in-situ test methods pertaining to geotechnical engineering and analysis of in-situ test results, including drilling and sampling, standard penetration test (SPT), cone-penetration test (CPT), piezocone penetration test (CPTu), vane shear test (VST), non-destructive tests (NDT) using body waves and surface waves - seismic reflection test, seismic refraction test, and spectral analysis of surface waves (SASW) test. Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs will be discussed. The contents of this course will enable students to utilize different in-situ test results for soil property interpretation, direct and indirect applications for the design of geotechnical structures, and liquefaction assessment. This course will be helpful to students when they start working as practicing engineers or for further graduate-level advanced courses in geotechnical engineering. Scope and Objective: Introduction to in-situ testing, drilling, and sampling, advantages and disadvantages of in-situ testing, and scope of using the test results for direct and indirect design of geotechnical structures. • Learn about SPT, test procedure, SPT corrections, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Become familiar with some of the frequently used methods for the design of foundations using SPT data. • Learn about CPT, test procedure, and frequently used correlations to estimate different geomaterial properties. • Design of foundations based on CPT results. • Assess liquefaction potential for a site based on SPT and CPT results. • Estimate seismic wave velocities and interpret subsurface profiles based on seismic reflection and refraction tests, and SASW test. • Structure and components of geotechnical reports and data presentation techniques using borehole logs based on exploration findings will be discussed. Course Learning Outcome: • Remember different in-situ testing methods related to geotechnical engineering. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division • Understanding of different widely used in-situ testing procedures and principles pertaining to geotechnical engineering. • Knowledge of appropriate correlation equations available to interpret different geomaterial properties using in-situ test results. • Apply different direct design methods for designing foundations. • Analyze and compare different in-situ test results for tests conducted at the same site and decide suitability of different test methods. • Evaluate the suitability of different test methods based on site details and purpose of testing, select suitable method for foundation design using in-situ test results and assess potential for liquefaction. 083_CE_F417.pdf.course_title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Civil Engineering
083_CE_F417.pdf.topics: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence and soft computing; Neural networks: Introduction, models, and its application in civil engineering, fuzzy logic and its application in decision making, Clustering; Genetic algorithms; Expert systems; Introduction to machine learning (Support Vector Machine), case studies. Scope and Objective: Artificial Intelligence (AI) may be considered a field of computer science that attempts to build technology to inculcate human cognition in computer systems, but applications are not limited to. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities. This course is structured to give an overview of the area, as well as some important soft computing techniques which are essential to solve the complex problems in terms of the fundamentals. The attributes of human intelligence such as reasoning, planning, learning etc. will be attempted to be understood to incorporate in problemsolving. Course learning outcomes: By the end of the course, the students should have a. Out of various techniques, emphasis will be on Genetic algorithm, Artificial Neural Network, and Fuzzy Systems a. General knowledge of the field of AI b. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve civil engineering problems. c. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter. d. Students will take up a group project/ term paper to study in detail the theoretical details of an intelligent system and implement that during the semester. Text books and references: TB1: Artificial Intelligence A Modern Approach; Stuart J.Russell, Peter Norvig, Third Edition Pearson Education, Inc., India TB2: Neural Networks, Fuzzy logic, and Genetic Algorithms Synthesis and Applications; S. 086_CE_G515.pdf.topics:
Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation, maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical, organizational, and stakeholder-related complexities by employing a holistic, systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure planning, development, and management. Students will explore systems architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop technically sound, system-aware professionals capable of solving real-world infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and evidence-based planning.

089_CE_G525.pdf.topics:
The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning and management of water resources. It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water systems, integrating surface and groundwater hydrology, water quality modeling, and watershed management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems. The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible water resource development and policy-making.

093_CE_G534.pdf.topics:
[as per the Bulletin] This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including soil, aggregates, bitumen,bituminous mixtures and pavement quality concrete (PQC). Soil characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification, compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade soil. For aggregates, origin and production, mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed. Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and it application, chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties, mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would be covered along with design example.

The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different lectures.

Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states. Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.

107_CE_G613.pdf.topics:
The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design of various elements and exposure to different code provisions. Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall buildings, detailing in concrete structures

The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind & earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins, nuclear reactors etc., The codal provisions are continuously changing with changing times due to technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete. Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding. ➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I] ➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II] ➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III] ➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV] ➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V] ➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI] ➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII] ➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII] 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division ➢ To discuss the case studies of differ ent RC structures and its failures [Module IX] ➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X]

109_CE_G614.pdf.topics:
Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders.

The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications. The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of practicing structural design engineers. The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members. This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed concrete structures.

111_CE_G616.pdf.topics:
Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges. This course will mainly focus on the design of three types of bridge superstructures namely Slab culverts/bridges, T-beam bridges, and Composite bridges. The design of the bridge substructure will include the design of elastomeric bearings and the design of abutments and piers. Moreover, the course will include the design aspects of continuous bridges. At the end of this course, the students would be equipped with the complete analysis and design of slab, T-beam and composite bridges, along with the design of substructures for them.

Purpose of bridge; Classification of bridges; Characteristics of different types of bridges; Loads stresses and their combinations; Design of RCC Slab culverts, Box-culverts, T-beam bridges; composite bridges; continuous bridges; design of bearings; design of piers and abutments and their foundations.

Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using computer oriented approach. The basic objective of this course is to acquire the fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures. By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized

Fundamentals of the finite element method (FEM); basic formulations of FEM; steps in FEM; 1-D, 2- D and 3-D elements; axi-symmetric elements, isoparametric formulations; programming aspects in FEM; plate bending elements; shell elements; material and geometric nonlinearity; Buckling and Vibration problems, application of FEM to civil engineering problems.

Finite element method is the most powerful numerical method widely used for solving problems in different branches of engineering especially Civil Engineering. This method is usually used to solve complex problems with regard to complexity in material, geometry, boundary, and loading conditions, such as non-homogeneous material, irregular geometry, boundary conditions, and static & dynamic loading conditions. The finite element formulation from the weak form of the governing differential equations is also covered. The course is aimed to enable students to understand the advanced concept of finite element method and its application to Civil Engineering.

Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of infrastructure projects: technical and procedural aspects, guidelines and legal aspects of environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA), dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk analysis methodologies; mitigation of environmental impacts; case studies; environmental management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are discussed with reference to national and international standards, including ISO, ensuring comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.

This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations, which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical process plants. Fundamentals of this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.

The main objective of this course is to familiarize the students on different principles of chemical engineering through hands on experimentation. The experiments are designed to enable students to apply the theoretical background assimilated in the relevant chemical engineering courses to practice in a laboratory environment. Emphasis is laid on employing scientific methodology in practice: each experiment requires planning, data collection, calculations based on chemical engineering principles, critical analysis, discussion and presentation of the observed result. Additionally, the students will also learn the operation of laboratory scale scientific equipment.

This course is to equip students with the knowledge of a variety of modern simulation methods at the atomic and molecular levels. The course will deal with several atomic and molecular simulation methods e.g., ab initio methods, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, Monte Carlo (MC) methods, free energy algorithms, coarse-graining, and multiscale methods. The course will provide hands-on training for simulations using GROMACS or LAMMPS or similar and hands-on simulations using any DFT packages such as VASP, Quantum Espresso or similar. The course also introduces concepts and algorithms based on programming languages (e.g., Matlab, C, C++, Molecular Modelling Software, and Visual Software). Case studies and examples of several real-life applications will be presented for all the simulation techniques.

This course aims to give an overall introduction to various types of particle-based simulation techniques in the sub-micro level phenomena with hands-on training. Currently, with the advances in computational tools, more and more industries/researchers are focusing on using computational tools to study material properties for various applications. The course will include computational multi-scale methods, from first principle ab initio calculations to molecular mechanics, offering potential pathways for studying advanced materials for several applications such as molecular electronics, energy storage/generation, separation, and purification, to name a few. After successful completion of the course, the students will be equipped with the theoretical basis and algorithms of several atomic and molecular simulations techniques (DFT, MD, MC) with their typical application areas and will be able to solve real- world problems by choosing the right simulation techniques.

Transport phenomena is one of the basic subjects of chemical engineering and includes study of fluid dynamics, heat and mass transfer. The governing equations for the aforementioned transport processes are analogous in nature as the underlying molecular mechanisms are very closely related. The objective of this course is to cover advance topics in this area like the transport of momentum, heat and mass in turbulent flow, creeping flows, flow through porous media, flow over flat plates and curved surfaces, interphase transport, etc. A balanced overview and fundamental equations for transport processes would be provided along with illustrations regarding solving relevant problems. Further, some special cases which are frequently encountered would also be covered.

The chemical industry has undergone significant changes during the past 25 years due to the increased cost of energy, increasingly stringent environmental regulations, and global competition in product pricing and quality. One of the most important engineering tools for addressing these issues is optimization. Optimization as the name suggests, deals with finding the optimum design parameters for maximizing the profit or minimizing the total investment on a process plant. The criteria for analysis of the economic objective function involve fulfilling a process criteria restrictions, conditions, design equations, and respecting the limits of the variables. Most problems in chemical engineering processes have many solutions, in some cases becoming endless. The optimization is related to the selection of an option that is best in a variety of efficient options but being the only one that comes closest to an economic optimum performance and operation. This course, as a subject, deals with the concepts of modeling & simulation, various methods of optimization, objective functions, constraints, theoretical & computational basis for optimization techniques, various chemical engineering examples, etc. The objective of the course is to apply the optimization techniques in chemical engineering processes for reducing the operating cost and maximizing the profit. After completing this course the students will be able to apply the principle of optimization in solving engineering problems and understand the scope of optimization in solving Chemical Engineering problems.

160_CS_F111.pdf.topics:
Basic model of computation, input, processing, output, and storage; problem decomposition, abstraction, and representation of solutions using flowcharts and pseudocode. Algorithmic thinking, formulation of algorithms, tracing and verification of correctness, and comparison of efficiency at a conceptual level. Programming fundamentals, expressions, variables, primitive and composite data types, type conversion, and operator precedence; conditional statements and structured decision making; bounded and unbounded iteration. Modular program design, functions, parameter passing, scope, and structured program development. Recursion, recursive problem solving, base and recursive cases, call stack behaviour, and comparison with iterative approaches. Data structures, arrays, strings, and structured data representations; pointers, dynamic memory allocation, and memory management. File handling, basic input/output operations and sequential data processing. AI-assisted programming, responsible use of AI tools for code generation, including prompt formulation, critical evaluation, debugging, and verification of generated code. Laboratory: Algorithm design and tracing; implementation of programs involving conditionals, iteration, functions, recursion, arrays, strings, structured data, pointers, and dynamic memory; file handling; and integrated problem-solving exercises with critical evaluation of AI-assisted code.

This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail, express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: ● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. ● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. ● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. ● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. ● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution.

165_CS_F317.pdf.topics:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) is based on the idea where we learn by interacting with our environment. It is a collection of machine learning techniques where agent(s) learn how to behave in an environment by performing actions and assessing the results. RL approach is building programs that learn how to predict and act in stochastic environment, based on experience. This course will provide an overview to students on some of the fundamental ideas on which modern RL is built including Markov decision processes, Mult-armed bandits value functions, Monte Carlo estimation, dynamic programming, TD methods, approximation methods, Actor-Critic methods, etc. This course will help students to understand and apply RL in several systems including video distribution systems, game development, IOT devices, robotics, clinical decision making, industrial process control, finance portfolio balancing, etc.

This course aims to achieve the following goals: • To provide students with the knowledge to structure a reinforcement learning problem. • To introduce students to learn and apply basic RL algorithms for simple sequential decision-making problems in uncertain conditions • To introduce students research and development work in reinforcement learning by interpreting state-of-the-art RL research and communicating their results. • To provide knowledge to students to build a RL system that knows how to make automated decisions. • To give students opportunities to understand the space of RL algorithms including Temporal Difference Learning, Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, approximation solution methods, A2C, A3C, etc.

167_CS_F342.pdf.topics: This course develops a comprehensive understanding of computer architecture and organization, from quantifying processor performance to designing a working processor and its supporting memory system. It begins with performance measurement and comparison using key metrics, benchmarking tools, and Amdahl's law. Building on this, it covers the MIPS architecture and instruction set. The course then examines the design of single-cycle and multi-cycle processor. It further explores pipelined processor design, the handling of structural, data, and control hazards through forwarding, stalling, reordering, and branch prediction techniques. The memory hierarchy is studied to exploit locality of reference, covering memory technologies, cache mapping functions, cache controller design, cache performance metrics, and multi-level caches. Finally, the course introduces advanced techniques for increasing instruction-level parallelism, including multiple issue, loop unrolling, speculation, and dynamic scheduling. TEXT BOOKS (T1) Patterson, David A & J L Hennenssy, Computer Organisation & Design, Elsevier, 6 Ed., 2021. th (T2) Samir Palnitkar, Verilog HDL: A Guide to Digital Design and Synthesis, Pearson Education Asia, 2nd Ed. 2006. 170_CS_F407.pdf.topics: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a field of computer science that seeks to build systems that emulate human cognition. A primary goal of AI is to build intelligent entities that mimic human intelligence, such as problem-solving, reasoning, planning, uncertainty handling, and learning. By the end of the course, the students should have a general knowledge of the field of AI. They should be able to recognize when and how to use AI techniques to solve problems. The students should also be able to evaluate new techniques they encounter. This course covers the issues and techniques involved in creating computer systems that exhibit intelligent behavior. Introduction to Data Mining, fundamental concepts; motivation and applications; role of data warehousing in data mining; challenges and issues in data mining; Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD); role of data mining in KDD; algorithms for data mining; tasks like decision-tree construction, finding association rules, sequencing, classification, and clustering; applications of neural networks and machine learning for tasks of classification and clustering.

The course explores the concepts and techniques of data mining, a promising and flourishing frontier in database systems. Data Mining is automated extraction of patterns representing knowledge implicitly stored in large databases, data warehouses, and other massive information repositories. It is a decision support tool that addresses unique decision support problems that cannot be solved by other data analysis tools such as Online Analytical Processing (OLAP). The course covers data mining tasks like constructing decision trees, finding association rules, classification, and clustering. The course is designed to provide students with a broad understanding in the design and use of data mining algorithms. The course also aims at providing a holistic view of data mining. It will have database, statistical, algorithmic and application perspectives of data mining.

This course establishes computational problem solving as a discipline before it establishes programming as a skill. Students first learn to decompose a problem, abstract away detail, express a solution as an algorithm, and reason about its correctness and cost. They then learn to realise those solutions as working programs, progressing from control structures and modular design to recursion, structured data, pointers, and explicit memory management. The course is anchored in C so that students build an accurate mental model of storage, addressing, and program execution, which is the model assumed by subsequent courses in data structures, operating systems, computer architecture, and networks. This subject aims to achieve the following goals: ● To develop the ability to decompose problems, abstract essential detail, and express solutions as algorithms independent of any programming language. ● To build fluency in structured programming, covering data types, expressions, control constructs, and modular function design. ● To establish an accurate mental model of program execution and memory through recursion, pointers, and dynamic memory management. ● To develop competence in representing and processing structured and linked data, and in persisting data through file operations. ● To build the judgement required to evaluate, test, and verify AI-generated code, and to use AI programming tools responsibly and with due attribution.

Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization

This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

Scope and objective of the course: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of electromagnetic wave theory and microwave engineering, focusing on Maxwell’s equations, wave propagation, and transmission line theory. It covers the analysis and design of waveguides, cavity resonators, and dielectric structures. Students will explore microwave devices, S-parameters, impedance matching techniques, and measurement methods. The course also introduces microwave generators, amplifiers, and various types of antennas with their characteristics. The objective is to equip students with the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to analyze, design, and apply high-frequency systems in modern communication, radar, and sensing applications. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to analyze electromagnetic wave propagation using Maxwell’s equations, understand wave behavior at interfaces, and design transmission lines with impedance matching using the Smith Chart. They will gain proficiency in characterizing waveguides, cavity resonators, and microwave devices, as well as interpreting S- parameters for network analysis. Students will also learn measurement techniques, explore microwave sources and amplifiers, and evaluate various antenna types and their radiation characteristics for practical applications.

Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.

The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.

Businesses are the driving force behind a nation's economic activity since they enable its population to attain a higher quality of living. It is essential to understand that a business firm does not operate in a vacuum but in a given environment and must interact and transact its business within this environment. Business environment refers to the totality of all individuals, institutions, and other forces external to a business unit but potentially affecting its performance. Business enterprises are micro units within an economic environment that represents the macro. The economic environment is the “given” within which firms and their managements must operate. So, the business environment and the manner and effectiveness of the interaction of an enterprise with its environment would generally determine its success or failure.

The course aims to (1) Create familiarity with economic environment concepts and indicators, economic policies, and economic regulation (2) Develop the ability to analyze and anticipate changes in the economic environment and, (3) Enable students to take more effective business decisions by being responsive to the changing external economic environment. The objective of this course is to unravel all those economic factors that are external to and beyond the control of individual business enterprises and their management, with a focus on the Indian context.

This course provides a comprehensive and contemporary examination of the major issues, challenges, and policy debates in economic development by integrating theoretical perspectives, empirical evidence, and real-world applications. It views development as a multidimensional process that extends beyond economic growth to encompass structural transformation, human development, institutional quality, technological progress, environmental sustainability, and social inclusion. The course explores why countries experience divergent development trajectories and examines the roles of markets, governments, institutions, globalization, and technological change in shaping long- run development outcomes. Drawing upon classical and contemporary development theories, with particular emphasis on India and other developing economies, the course examines a broad range of development issues, including poverty, inequality, unemployment, population dynamics, demographic transition, migration, urbanization, education, health, agriculture, industrialization, infrastructure, financial inclusion, foreign investment, governance, environmental degradation, climate change, artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Through analytical frameworks, empirical evidence, policy debates, and case studies, students will develop the ability to critically examine development challenges, interpret development indicators, and evaluate alternative policy interventions for achieving sustainable, inclusive, and equitable development.

The primary objective of this course is to equip students with a rigorous understanding of the theoretical, empirical, and policy dimensions of economic development while fostering the analytical skills required to evaluate contemporary development challenges. The course enables students to understand the economic, social, institutional, technological, and environmental factors that influence development outcomes across countries and regions. It emphasizes the interrelationships among economic growth, structural transformation, employment generation, poverty reduction, income distribution, human capital formation, institutional development, and environmental sustainability. Students will critically examine competing development theories and policy paradigms, evaluate the effectiveness of development strategies adopted by different countries, and analyze the role of public policy in promoting inclusive and sustainable development. The course also introduces emerging issues that are reshaping development discourse, including artificial intelligence and development, digital transformation, climate resilience, financial inclusion, gender equality, governance, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Equal emphasis is placed on developing students' analytical, quantitative, and research competencies through the interpretation of development indicators, evaluation of empirical evidence, policy analysis, and application of contemporary development concepts to real- world economic issues. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to critically assess development policies and contribute to evidence-based decision-making in both academic and policy contexts. 1 Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani Pilani | Dubai | Goa | Hyderabad ACADEMIC— UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION

223_ECON_F315.pdf.topics:
Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division

This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.
