224_ECON_F354.pdf.topics: The objective of this course is to provide students an introductory level familiarity with a particular type of financial instruments known as DERIVATIVES. To achieve the stated objectives, the course provides a detailed description on the structure (read, design) and utility (read, relevance) of the most common and popular financial derivatives namely, Options, Futures, and Swaps. The scope of the course entails acquainting students with the mechanics of trading and settlement of derivative instruments in the financial markets and their function as insurance products for hedging financial risk. No understanding about financial instruments or their derivatives is complete without a thorough grasp over interest rate concepts and hence the course also includes discussion on topics such as time value of money, term structure of interest rates and their role in valuation of bonds, computation of yield and forward interest rates, estimating bond-price volatility, and the role of bond duration and convexity in mitigating interest rate risks. The topics covered in the course will, at an introductory level, enable participants to learn about common risks prevalent in the financial markets and how to manage its impact on investment exposure by using derivatives. Discussion on valuation of financial derivatives and a brief introduction to creating synthetic investment positions by combining derivatives prepares students for advanced level courses such as Financial Engineering and Financial Risk Analytics and Management. The course concludes with a survey of selective topics of contemporary interest to risk management industry such as forecasting volatility, estimating value-at-risk, etc. The topics covered in the course will also assist students in preparing for competitive professional international certifications such as Financial Risk Manager (FRM) and Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA).

225_ECON_F355.pdf.topics:
This course focuses on the essential tools and frameworks for evaluating the value of companies through financial analysis. Students will explore key concepts such as internal growth, mergers and acquisitions, along with valuation methodologies like discounted cash flow and relative valuation. Designed for those with prior knowledge in finance and accounting, the course equips students with the skills to analyze financial statements, assess market conditions, and identify key performance drivers. Ideal for aspiring professionals in investment banking, corporate finance, and consulting, this course enhances analytical capabilities and strategic thinking in business valuation and decision-making.

The Process of measuring and managing the value of companies is a central aspect of financial analysis. Globally, managers are in pursuit of adding value to their firms via two important means. One, by enhancing the firm’s productive capacity through internal (or organic) growth, which has a simultaneous positive impact on its stock price. Second, through mergers and acquisitions (a decision involving factors external to the firm) that interlocks with corporation’s key strengths, and yield benefits in the long run. Hence, asking, “What is something worth?” is a vital question to business decision making, and the principal objective behind this course is to provide the learners with the conceptual basis, intuitive reasoning, and analytical framework to answer this question. The focus of this course is on valuing equity (or ownership) in a firm and estimating the value of the overall enterprise. The coverage relies on discounted cash flow, relative valuation, and contingent valuation approaches for extracting the value of a business. Since financial statements serve as the basis for all types of valuation methods, the course begins by providing brief framework on the principles governing the financial statements, and adjustments that are often required to capture the underlying business reality. Students who are either currently pursuing or would like to embark on a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting will find the course material to be most useful. The course also carries a broader appeal to individuals who are interested in enhancing their understanding of financial analysis, and in learning how businesses measure and create value for their investors. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Important: This is not a beginning level course. The course presumes that you have a prior exposure on a variety of introductory concepts in finance, accounting, and statistics. For beginners, it is therefore highly recommended that they go through the introductory material in finance and accounting concepts at the earliest. Feel free to contact the I/C ASAP in case you are facing difficulty in following the classroom discussions.

226_ECON_F412.pdf.topics:
Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.

The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture. In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3) go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest- lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.

NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence, the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key external partners?

233_EE_G508.pdf.topics:
Urban Water Management is an advanced course focusing on the planning, design, operation, and assessment of urban water systems under increasing pressures of population growth, urbanization, and climate change. It explores the complete urban water cycle, including supply, sanitation, drainage, and environmental flows, with strong emphasis on sustainable and resilient urban development. The course addresses technical, social, economic, and regulatory challenges through a multidisciplinary lens. Students are exposed to contemporary topics such as stormwater management, water-sensitive urban design, and water quality monitoring. Practical software-based training modules on stormwater modelling, flood forecasting, and hydroinformatics are integrated to bridge theory and real-world applications. Students will also gain insights into advanced asset management systems, sustainability indicators, GIS tools, and the effect of urbanization on hydrological behavior. This industry-oriented course prepares students for professional roles in government, consulting, and research sectors concerned with smart, equitable, and sustainable urban water solutions.

The course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in managing urban water systems effectively and sustainably. The scope spans water supply, sanitation, stormwater, groundwater, and urban drainage management. It incorporates key concepts in water-sensitive urban design, reuse and recycling of wastewater, climate-resilient infrastructure planning, and integrated urban water modelling. Emphasis is placed on understanding emerging urban water challenges, regulatory frameworks, and digital tools for decision support. Through hands-on sessions, case studies, and software exposure, the course objectives are: (1) To understand the integrated urban water cycle and its components; (2) To develop competence in water quality and infrastructure assessment; (3) To analyze risks and sustainability indicators in urban water systems; (4) To apply hydroinformatics tools for modeling and performance evaluation; and (5) To foster decision-making skills relevant to urban water management, policies, and climate adaptation strategies.

Topics include source coding, channel coding, baseband and passband modulation techniques, receiver design, and channel equalization

This course intends to cover the basic understanding of functionalities of various block-sets involved in communication system. Course starts with an overview of communication systems, communication process, generic model and block diagram description. The course also reviews important concepts of signal and systems, and random variables which are useful for understanding and analyzing communication systems. The course covers both analog and digital communication systems. The course also covers information theoretic approach to deal with the random additive noise. The course deals with analog and digital modulation schemes in a deterministic way as well as analyzes the effect of random noise on the performance of communication systems. The course introduces performance metrics such as SNR and BER and performance limits of communications for both analog (using Nyquist rate) and digital (using Shannon theorem). The course has a lab component which includes simulation experiments for analog and digital communication systems using MATLAB and Python software. The objective of the course is to equip students with fundamental understanding to model, design, and analyze analog and digital communication systems for various practical scenarios. This course will serve as a basis to learn advanced level courses on communications and develop physical layer algorithms. Students will be given assignments on communication system modeling using MATLAB and Python. Students are expected to have an understanding of Signals and Systems, Electronic Devices and Circuits, Mathematics, and basics of Electromagnetic Field Theory.

250_EEE_F422.pdf.topics: Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so- called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments drawn from various engineering domains.

251_EEE_F426.pdf.topics:
Optical communication systems and components; optical sources and transmitters (basic concept, design and applications); modulators (electro- optic, acousto-optic and laser modulation techniques); beam forming; focusing and coupling schemes to optical repeaters; optical amplifiers; optical field reception; coherent and non-coherent light wave systems; fiber optic communication system design and performance; multichannel light wave systems; long haul communications; fiber optic networks.

In the recent past, tremendous advances have been achieved in fiber optics and associated optoelectronics. These developments have made fiber - optic communication synonymous with the current worldwide revolution in information technology. This course aims at providing the students with a firm grounding in the major aspects of this emerging technology. Thus the course deals with the study of various building blocks of fiber optic systems, e.g. optical fibers, sources, detectors, modulators, optical amplifiers, etc. together with overall system design and performance analysis for communication applications.

253_EEE_F435.pdf.topics:
This is the first course on digital image processing. It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of digital images and discusses the various discrete transformations, which are extensively used in image processing. It then goes on to discuss the different image processing techniques such as image enhancement, automatic image classification, and recognition.

Digital Image Processing (DIP) involves the use of computer algorithms to perform operations on digital images to improve their quality, extract useful information, or prepare them for further analysis. The main objectives of DIP include enhancing image details for better visual interpretation, restoring corrupted images, compressing image data for efficient storage and transmission, and analyzing images for applications like medical diagnosis, satellite imaging, and object recognition. Its scope spans various fields such as healthcare, agriculture, surveillance, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence, making it a vital tool in both scientific research and everyday technology.

254_EEE_F437.pdf.topics:
The course describes both theoretical and practical aspects of semiconductor fabrication technology. This course will take you on the journey of silica sand to silicon integrated circuit (IC), i.e., “making a chip”. Converting a single crystal of silicon into an IC requires several fabrication steps, such as epitaxy, oxidation, chemical vapor deposition, metallization, ion implantation, diffusion, etching, and lithography. All these process steps will be discussed. Further, the modeling of each processing step would be discussed in detail.

This course is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of semiconductor fabrication and to discuss various processing technologies. Fabrication of semiconductor chips is a joint venture by electrical engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges across various disciplines.

This course introduces satellite communication systems, combining radio-wave propagation, or- bital mechanics, satellite subsystems, modulation, and coding. Satellite link analysis and link- budget design form the core, applied hands-on component of the course, reinforced through in-class problem-solving sessions and selected simulation tasks. Students then study fixed- assignmentmultiple-accesstechniques(FDMA/TDMA/CDMA)andbrieflyexplorerandom-access schemes, followed by applications in VSAT, mobile satellite, and GPS/DGPS. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyze satellite communication systems, able to design satellite links and evaluate their performance, develop and defend a link-budget analysis, and determine satellite position/coverage for a given orbit.

263_EEE_G515.pdf.topics:
This course will introduce the general concepts related to real-time systems from introduction, to designing a real-time system (RTS). It will deal will a reference model of an RTS which can be applied to any RTS. It will also teach the scheduling algorithms, resource management techniques, issues in hardware and software design, Real-Time Operating System (RTOS), advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems.

Real-time systems are those systems that require a deterministic upper time-bound for the execution of a job. With the proliferation of the embedded system, which is the heart of items ranging from common every day appliances to life-critical systems, a great deal of work has gone into the characterization and design issues of Real-time systems. The course focuses on the basics of Hardware design, advanced concepts of software design and validation techniques for these systems. Specifically we discuss the Operating system, Scheduling, Software techniques, Run-time environment, failure management algorithms, Reliability and Fault-tolerance of real-time systems etc.

The objective of the course is to comprehend and analyse the steady-state, transient and dynamic behaviour of electrical machines using mathematical models, and also to familiarize the students about advanced modelling. The course will develop students’ understanding on modelling of electrical machines from conventional methods to advanced methods through generalized theory of electrical machines. Furthermore, the students will appreciate the scope and applicability of course with the help of hands-on practice using simulation tools and hardware setup, encouraging and strengthening their ability to approach and investigate important challenges of automation and e-mobility associated to research interests of industries and academia, for example, digital-twin, model predictive modelling and control, fault analysis, predictive maintenance, and advanced control. The prerequisite of this course is, to have a basic understanding of electrical circuits, electrical machines and control systems; mainly modelling of physical systems.

This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-current- switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course.

a. Understand the concept of resonant tank network b. Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance c. Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter d. Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching

273_EEE_G593.pdf.topics:
This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations, harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries. The objectives of this course are designed to help students to: a. Understand various power quality issues and their impact. b. Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems. c. Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and load voltage regulation d. Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination. e. Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable energy systems. Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology.

This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover, integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors, quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/ simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

287_FIN_F212.pdf.topics:
Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails two important and interrelated aspects, i.e., a. Recording transactions, and b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc. Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing financial statements. The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership, credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold, recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets. This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance. Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the field of finance.

The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course accomplishes enables participants in learning: a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical to day-to-day functioning of the company. b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement of income etc. c. the key components that form part of these financial statements. d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.

288_FIN_F313.pdf.topics:
Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold. The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental, quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy, industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation forms a major component of this course. Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes: a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to: • Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics. • Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance management. • Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation. • Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques. • Technical analysis. • Financial derivative contracts and their applications.

289_FIN_F315.pdf.topics:
Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm. In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements, the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of fault lines in the financial markets. To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment, investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy. The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital, investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies. 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division

This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to: a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations, b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices. Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing, investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability. Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities, statistics, and MS-Excel.

290_FIN_F414.pdf.topics:
This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry. The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk management roles. Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory, Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering, Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk with Derivatives.

The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document.

This Course introduces certain select concepts of Politics that are relevant to the Modern/ Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political thought. This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and its execution emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical skills, and the understanding of human diversity. Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’ knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political discourses. Scope: As an introductory course in Politics, this is based on lectures and reading texts. However, the students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division values. 306_GS_F313.pdf.topics:
This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.

Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without fundamentally exploitative structures.

Introduction to social research: nature, purpose, relevance, dimensions, and the research process. Quantitative, qualitative, mixed methods, and triangulation. Social theory, ideology, positivist, interpretivist, critical, feminist, and postmodern perspectives. Research ethics and research design. Measurement, reliability, validity, scales, and sampling. Experimental, survey, field, historical-comparative, and nonreactive research methods. Data collection techniques, questionnaire design, interviewing, content analysis, and secondary data analysis. Quantitative and qualitative data analysis, coding, concept formation, inferential statistics, and report writing. Research analytics and software applications: statistical analysis using SPSS and Jamovi; qualitative coding and thematic analysis using NVivo; bibliometric, scientometric, and science mapping using Graphica (e.g., knowledge network visualization and research analytics).

This course seeks to provide knowledge and skills relevant for conducting social science research. It will cover the entire research process from problem formulation, interpretation of data (both qualitative and quantitative) to evaluation of research study. The course will also address fundamental social science issues, reasoning and approaches that govern certain methodologies. This course would help students in acquiring skills to undertake social research studies based on primary and/or secondary data.

 Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism; World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11, China’s entry into WTO.  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and Global Governance  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR  India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and United States.

International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations between the states and non-state actors. This course offers a critical reflection and analytical understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.

The course gives a humanistic perspective on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well- being of our planet.

Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science, engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues to address and various approaches to choose from: Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions? Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances. Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of solutions and do not require solving the differential equation. Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we change parameters in the differential equation (parameter dependence). Course helps deeper understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.

371_MATH_F421.pdf.topics: Combinatorics is often described briefly as being about counting, and indeed counting is a large part of combinatorics. As the name suggests, however, it is broader than this: it is about combining things. Questions that arise include counting problems: “How many ways can these elements be combined?” But there are other questions, such as whether a certain combination is possible, or what combination is the “best” in some sense. This course presents the different methods to solve the counting problems. We will mainly focus on combinatorial approach instead of algebraic approach. SCOPE and OBJECTIVES: Combinatorics is a fascinating and a broad subject. It’s hard to classify Combinatorics, but a common theme is that it deals with structures that are, in some sense, finite or discrete. What sets Combinatorics apart from other branches of Mathematics is that it focuses on techniques rather than results. The way a Theorem is proved is of bigger importance than the statement of the Theorem itself. Combinatorial reasoning underlies all analysis of Computer Systems. It plays a similar role in Discrete Operation Research Problems and in Finite Probability. It is very much useful in the analysis of the speed and logical structure of Operation Research Algorithms to optimize efficient manufacturing or garbage collections. It has been proven an efficient tool for Graph Counting. COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES: The course focuses on different techniques related to counting problems. At the end of the course, student will be aware of many existing methods used to solve counting problems and when these methods are applicable. 384_ME_F317.pdf.topics: The internal combustion engine (IC) is a heat engine that converts chemical energy in a fuel into mechanical energy, usually made available on a rotating output shaft. This is one of the dominating areas in prime movers. These engines are often used for the propulsion of a vehicle (i.e., automobile, truck, locomotive, marine vessel, or aeroplane), and other applications include stationary engines to drive generators or pumps and portable engines for things like chain saws and lawnmowers, etc. This course will introduce the students to system-level design concepts and the workings of internal combustion engines. Furthermore, electric mobility has become an essential part of the energy transition. This course focuses on the fundamentals of the technology behind electric vehicles. It will cover the contents such as the working principle of electric vehicles and delve into its key components, e.g. motors and power electronics, battery technology, charging technologies and future trends in the development of electric vehicles. 386_ME_F323.pdf.topics:
This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems, supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.

The objective of this course is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic, electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations, performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.

391_ME_F428.pdf.topics:
The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological fluids; magnetostrictive and electrostrictive materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural- health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus- responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms, observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research- oriented work in smart materials and structures.

394_ME_G511.pdf.topics: This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future. The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics, computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into the design methodologies, practical implementation principles, and real-world industrial applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain. Text Book: (T1) Mittal R. K. & Nagrath, I. J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later). Reference Books: (R1) Groover, M. P., et al., “Industrial Robotics”, McGraw Hill ISE, 1986. (R2) Fu, K. S., et al., Robotic: Control, Sensing, Vision & Intelligence, McGraw Hill ISE, 1987 (R3) Robert J., Schilling, Fundamentals of Robotics: Analysis and Control, Prentice Hall, NJ, 2002. _

402_ME_G552.pdf.topics:
This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics include principles of robot kinematics, statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation and precision assembly; sensor-integrated robotic systems; collaborative robotics; robotic work-cell implementation; and case studies and applications of industrial robots in intelligent manufacturing environments.

This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis, and operation of industrial robotic manipulators. Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and intelligent production systems. Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using industrial-grade platforms. Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: CO1 Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic manipulators. CO2 Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and- place, assembly, and material handling. CO3 Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with closed-loop control. CO4 Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions. _

This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic- moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components. Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry.

It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies.

411_MEL_G623.pdf.topics:
The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621 VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.

The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices. Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages of the design of a modern digital system.

413_MEL_G624.pdf.topics:
The course explores advanced VLSI processor architectures, their implementation strategies (microarchitectures) and associated memory hierarchies and their microarchitectures for high-performance system design. It also covers the various techniques utilized to leverage parallelism at hardware, application and compiler levels. Students will gain an understanding of how (beyond instruction-level parallelism) data-level parallelism, thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism can be exploited to architect and implement different processing cores e.g.: Vector Processors, SIMD processors and Multimedia processors, Graphical Processing Units (GPU) and Multi-core processors, Domain Specific Processors, and Memory hierarchy organizations for the above processors. The course also explores the emerging research directions in VLSI processor design and system architectures.

The objective of the course is to understand and gain an in-depth view of Advanced VLSI Architectures, specifically to study various processor architectures, associated microarchitectures, and memory organizations that have evolved to exploit different types of parallelism to increase processor performance. The scope of the course covers the following in detail: a. Study of advanced processor architectures and associated implementation techniques (microarchitectures) and memory organization techniques b. This includes the study of Vector, SIMD, GPU, and Domain Specific architectures and implementations c. Study of architectures and implementations that exploit thread-level parallelism and task-level parallelism via multi-processing (includes multicore processors) d. Study of memory hierarchy design for CPUs, vector processors, GPUs, and application domain-specific processors

other_instructors: Prof. Chandra Shekhar, Dr. Govind Prasad

In factories around the globe, Toyota consistently raises the bar for manufacturing, product development and process excellence. The result is an amazing business success story: steadily taking market share from price- cutting competitors, earning far more profit than any other automaker, and wining the praise of business leaders worldwide. Today business around the world is attempting to implement Toyota system to maintain competitive advantage. But are they? You will discover how the right combination of long- term philosophy, processes, people and problem solving can transform your organization into a lean, learning enterprise – the Toyota way. 437_MPBA_G503.pdf.topics:
This basic course in marketing is designed to familiarize students with the strategic and tactical decision making process in marketing that deals with the fundamental goal of creating, communicating and delivering value to the customer. This requires a professional knowledge of market drivers, competitors’ capabilities, technological trends and the market dynamics of value. The focus will be on the imbibing the skills of uncovering market opportunities by asking certain strategic questions.

On successful completion of this course, participants will be able to critically analyze and intelligently draw inference about the marketing strategies of organizations. Through an intensive assignment an effort will be made to develop the necessary skills for crafting a typical marketing plan grounded in real world data. Finally, awareness of tools available to marketing managers to facilitate planning and decision-making would be one of the gains from the course. Students are encouraged to bring some of the topical issues of contemporary concern in marketing to the classroom for discussion. Students will also be expected to imbibe path-breaking classic marketing literature in a group setting through group discussions for a sound academic base. A number of journal articles will be discussed in this course to give the course its academic rigor. The course pedagogy lays special emphasis on “learning by doing” through regular discussion of 6-7 Harvard Business Review cases as well as through a group marketing project assignment.

439_MPBA_G504.pdf.topics:
The course studies human behavior in organizations at three levels: individual, group, and organizational systems. It examines variables and key concepts related to individual attitudes, motivation, and leadership, along with group dynamics, organizational structure, and change management, while also covering the strategic role of HRM in attracting, developing, motivating, and retaining talent through recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, employee engagement, compensation, and talent management.

In the contemporary time, organizations across the world are facing economic and social consequences of global economic pressures and globalization. Under such scenario, they encounter many challenges and get various opportunities as well. Moreover, management of these challenges and opportunities has become crucial which essentially relies on an understanding of human behavior. The success of any organization in today's dynamic and volatile business environment is dependent upon the motivation and commitment of its employees. It is in this context the significance of organizational behavior comes into play. As people from diverse backgrounds and with different cultural values have to work together in the global economy, the study of organizational behavior assumes greater importance and relevance. This course focuses on the fundamental theories of behavior in organizations and managing employees in organizations with the objective of equipping students with the necessary concepts, tools, and techniques for understanding behavior in organizations, this course attempts to unfold human behavior at three levels (the individual, the group, and the organization). This course involves active learning and develops students' foundation against which the competencies required to create a successful organization can be built and developed.

441_MPBA_G505.pdf.topics:
Probability and Probability Distributions, Characteristics of Probability Distributions, Some Important Probability Distributions, statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing; ANOVA, MANOVA, MANCOVA, the linear regression model (two-variable model, multiple regression, functional forms, dummy variables); regression analysis in practice (model selection criteria and tests, multicollinearity, heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation), simultaneous-equations models. Statistical package 'R' will be used in this course.

This course serves as an introductory exploration of statistical analysis and fundamental econometrics, wherein the principles of economic theory, mathematics, and statistical inference are employed to examine business phenomena. The curriculum encompasses a review of probability distributions, statistical inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing. It also covers analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and introduces multiple regression analysis, which remains the most widely utilized statistical technique within the field of econometrics. The latter part of the course addresses various practical considerations related to linear regression models, including the use of dummy variables, alternative functional forms, and the implications of violating classical regression assumptions. Students will engage in the study and application of regression analysis to diverse data sets, thereby gaining familiarity with core concepts such as the estimation of economic parameters, forecasting business outcomes, and conducting statistical inference. A weekly two-hour laboratory session will be conducted, during which students will learn to explore and analyze different types of economic data using R programming. This component aims to develop proficiency in advanced statistical and econometric techniques through practical applications in R.

443_MPBA_G506.pdf.topics:
This course introduces students to the practical usage of databases, emphasizing SQL. As big data problems become more prevalent for businesses, this module introduces the basics of databases. After successful completion of the course, students will be able to learn why database management is essential, analyze the data requirements of a business scenario and represent these requirements utilizing entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, translate an ER diagram into normalized tables for a relational database management system, and write simple and relatively complex data retrieval queries. Students will learn how to extract valuable insights from databases through data analytics powered by SQL.

The course covers various Database Management and Data Warehousing concepts and enhances learning effectiveness through developing scripting skills. It aims to provide students with the necessary knowledge and skills to understand the data infrastructure underpinning business intelligence and analytics. Students undertaking this course should be able to appreciate the complexities involved in Database management and be prepared to solve the issues a business analyst faces. 3 . Course learning outcomes:  Understand the database environment and the complete development process, including requirements gathering, design, and implementation.  Model data using Entity-Relationship diagrams and design logical and physical relational databases.  Write effective SQL queries to manage and manipulate data within relational databases.  Explain the architecture of database applications, foundations of data warehousing, and principles of data quality and integration.  Explore the role of databases in Big Data analytics and understand essential tasks in database administration.

This course offers an introduction to deep learning and its practical relevance in business contexts. It covers foundational concepts such as neural networks, linear and logistic regression using neural architectures, deep neural networks, hyperparameter tuning, and advanced models like CNNs, RNNs, LSTMs, GANs, and deep reinforcement learning. The course blends theoretical understanding with hands-on applications to solve real-world business problems. It also highlights the challenges and limitations of deep learning methods in practice.

The course aims to equip students with foundational and practical knowledge of deep learning algorithms and their applications in solving business challenges. The course emphasizes: a. Understanding core deep learning architectures and techniques b. Translating business problems into machine learning tasks c. Developing, training, and tuning deep learning models using appropriate tools d. Applying deep learning to solve business challenges e. Utilizing TensorFlow and Keras libraries on Google Colab to implement and explore deep learning algorithms f. Recognizing the limitations, ethical concerns, and interpretability issues of deep models in business decision-making g. Engaging in a group-based project, where students apply deep learning techniques to some real- world business problems

449_MPBA_G515.pdf.topics: Prescriptive analytics is the third and final phase of business analytics, which also includes descriptive and predictive analytics. Referred to as the "final frontier of analytic capabilities", prescriptive analytics entails the application of mathematical and computational sciences and suggests decision options for how to take advantage of the results of descriptive and predictive phases. The first stage of business analytics is descriptive analytics, which still accounts for the majority of all business analytics today. Descriptive analytics looks at past performance and understands that performance by mining historical data to look for the reasons behind past success or failure. Most management reporting – such as sales, marketing, operations, and finance – uses this type of post- mortem analysis. The next phase is predictive analytics. Predictive analytics answers the question of what is likely to happen in the future. This is where historical data is combined with rules, algorithms, and occasionally external data to determine the probable future outcome of an event or the likelihood that a situation will occur. The final phase is prescriptive analytics, which goes beyond predicting future outcomes to suggest actions to benefit from those predictions and show the implications of each decision option. While the term prescriptive analytics was first coined by IBM and was later trademarked by Texas-based company Ayata, the underlying concepts have been around for hundreds of years in the form of Operations Research. Prescriptive Analytics has been considered the next step towards increasing data analytics maturity and leading to optimized, ahead-of-time decision-making for business performance improvement. New Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), such as the Internet of Things (IoT), real-time streaming, and sensor-driven business operations, have bolstered prescriptive analytics and provided businesses with accurate prescriptions, facilitating reliable and effective decision-making. Please Consider Your Environmental Responsibilities Do Not Print Unless Necessary BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHONOLOGY AND SCIENCE, PILANI Pilani Campus Prescriptive analytics assists the decision-maker in identifying the best action (optimal solution) given the problem context. The difference between decisions made using descriptive/predictive analytics and prescriptive analytics is that a prescriptive analytics algorithm seeks the best decision (optimal solution) based on an objective function (sometimes multiple objective functions) and a set of constraints. Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. Students can download a trial version (free) of Lingo from https://www.lindo.com/index.php/products/lingo-and-optimization-modeling Using Lingo, large-scale, complex Prescriptive Analytics problems can be solved.

Prescriptive analytics models attempt to solve complex optimization problems of the modern era. Students will be exposed to a powerful optimization software package, Lingo, so they can formulate and solve real-life Prescriptive Analytics problems. 456_MPBA_G524.pdf.topics: (Scope and Objective): This course equips students with the analytical frameworks, methods, and tools needed to make evidence-based marketing decisions across the customer lifecycle. It introduces the role of marketing analytics in supporting strategic and operational decisions, distinguishing business intelligence, analytics, and data science, and communicating insights through dashboards and data-driven storytelling. Students will apply analytical techniques to core marketing problems including customer segmentation and positioning, product and pricing analytics, market mix modeling, customer journey analysis, customer experience, retention and lifetime value, digital marketing measurement, and attribution. The course covers methods such as cluster analysis, multidimensional scaling, conjoint analysis, regression, price elasticity modeling, forecasting and diffusion models, principal component analysis, logistic regression, A/B testing, ANOVA, Bayesian networks, and optimization. The course also examines the growing role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, text and image analytics, recommender systems, personalization, and responsible generative AI in marketing. Emphasis is placed on practical interpretation and managerial application of results using tools such as Microsoft Excel, Power BI, DAX, and Python/R. By the end of the course, students will be able to translate marketing data into actionable insights, evaluate marketing performance, and develop data-informed recommendations for products, customers, channels, and brands. 463_MPBA_G532.pdf.topics:
A key component of financial management is the act of calculating and managing a company's value. In essence, managers work to increase the value of their companies in two ways: by increasing the firm's productivity through internal (or organic) growth and by making wise acquisitions that play to the company's core competencies. It follows that practically every significant business choice is decided by asking, "What is it worth?" This course's main goal is to arm you with the conceptual foundation, logical framework, and intuitive reasoning needed to make thoughtful decisions on company value. This course's emphasis is on asses ing the value of the entire enterprise and valuing stock in a company. For our study, we'll depend on the income and market approaches of financial valuation. The course begins by presenting a brief framework on the rules regulating financial statements and changes that are frequently needed to capture the underlying company reality because financial statements serve as the foundation for all types of valuation methodologies. We will use spreadsheet for building the financial model of a company. This course will be most helpful to students who are either pursuing a career in investment banking, corporate finance, venture capital, entrepreneurship, or business consulting or who would like to do so. The course also has a broader appeal to people who want to improve their

There will be three weekly classes. Class time will be devoted to lectures, role-plays, exercises, questionnaire, case discussions and videotapes. Lectures will provide analytical concepts that will integrate the readings and serve as useful framework for a richer understanding of cases and role-plays. Role-plays, cases and videotapes provide the "application" aspects of this course. People Analytics is the application of data science and information technology in the domain of Human resource management. The present course is designed to progress the understanding of the role of data-driven decisions about people's issues in an organization. This emerging discipline signifies the strategic role of HR function in the contemporary organizations. However, with the advent of analytics, it has evolved into a holistic function taking care of all people related aspects at the workplace, not only traditional HR operations. It serves as a key driver in pursuit of sustainable competitive advantage for organizations by leveraging data driven practices for an improved decision making. Grounded on 4Ts principle: Task, Theory, Technique, and Technology; the course integrates underlying theories and principles, and data analytical tools and techniques to drive business objectives. The course is structured to equip students with hands-on experience on analytical softwares to track, maintain, retrieve, analyze, and interpret HR data (e.g., staffing, skills, performance ratings and compensation information) to contribute to business outcomes. This will serve the twin purpose of elevating the students’ understanding on nuances of analytics in organizations, which will aid in students’ value addition and employability. The learning objectives of the course are as under:  This course introduces the student to the theory, concepts, and business application of human resources research, data, metrics, systems, analyses, and reporting. _

484_PHA_G538.pdf.topics: This course covers key immunologic concepts: how the components of the immune system are generated, organized, and function; the mechanisms that lead to beneficial immune responses, immune disorders, and immunodeficiencies; methods to identify immune reactions; and ways to manipulate the immune system and its components to benefit the patient. It will help the students to gain the necessary transferable and research skills in basic and clinical immunology to promote lifelong learning and career development.

490_PHA_G542.pdf.topics:
Physicochemical principles involved in effective formulation development, including various aspects like, pharmaceutical preformulation including bulk characteristics, polymorphism, solubility analysis, solid and solution state stability, compatibility. This course also cover various ICH guidelines like stability study, specifications, impurities which are required during formulation development. This course also discussed details about mechanical properties of powders, principles of dissolution, in-vitro in-vivo correlation (IVIVC), polymer science, etc.

Prior to the development of any dosage form with a new or old drug candidate, it is essential that certain fundamental physical and chemical properties of the drug molecule and other derived properties of the drug are determined. This information dictates possible approaches in formulation development. The aim of this course is to make the students understand those physicochemical principles which must be applied in the formulation and development of an efficacious dosage form, so that required duration and intensity of effect can be ensured at the intended site of action.

Overview of new drug research and development; Bioethics and institutional review board; regulatory control of clinical trials for NDA & ANDA application; Good Clinical Practice (GCP); related ICH guidelines; applied clinical epidemiology and biostatistics; clinical trial study design; trial development (protocol, case report form, and data management); clinical trial management- coordinating clinical trial at the site, documentation methodology, implementing monitoring plan and performing quality control; statistical analysis and data interpretation; monitoring obligations and methods; and Medical writing & report preparation for various submissions.

There is a growing need for clinical researchers in the health industries (pharmaceutical, biotechnology/medical device companies, research institutes, and hospitals) involved in the development of new drugs and therapies. This course is aimed at training students in conducting clinical trials on humans with new drugs/therapies before they are introduced to the market. Students completing the coursework will gain specialized knowledge and skills required to design, monitor, and manage clinical trials. Courses include the drug development process; regulations, guidelines, and standards; research methodology and biostatistics; clinical trial organization, monitoring, and documentation; and project management.

499_PHA_G618.pdf.topics:
This course deals with the strategy and tactics involved in the synthesis of organic molecules. The idea is to identify key structural features in the target molecules and then go backward logically to identify appropriate starting materials and chemical reactions for their synthesis. Knowledge and understanding of common organic reagents and reaction mechanisms are required for this course.

Most life-saving drugs are organic molecules. This course aims to develop a logical understanding which can be used to propose the synthesis of an organic compound. This course teaches various strategies and tactics together with the common nomenclature used in Retrosynthetic Analysis. At the end of the course, students should be able to propose a synthetic scheme for various drug molecules with appropriate justification.
