508_PHY_F211.pdf.topics: This course introduces the principles of classical mechanics from Newtonian and analytical perspectives. It covers constrained motion, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations, variational principles, central-force dynamics, canonical transformations, Poisson brackets, the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies in inertial, and rotating reference frames. Scope & Objectives: To provide a strong foundation in analytical mechanics and equip students with the mathematical and physical tools required to formulate, analyze, and solve problems in classical mechanics with elegance and rigor. Importantly, the course serves as a gateway to advanced topics in theoretical physics, including quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, electrodynamics, and general relativity. Course learning outcomes:  Apply vector calculus, generalized coordinates, and analytical methods to formulate and solve problems involving the motion of particles and systems with constraints using Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations.  Analyze central-force motion and variational principles to derive equations of motion, identify conserved quantities, investigate orbital dynamics and stability, and explain the role of symmetries in classical mechanics.  Employ Hamiltonian mechanics, canonical transformations, generating functions, and Poisson brackets to transform, simplify, and solve dynamical systems while recognizing canonical invariants.  Evaluate the kinematics and dynamics of rigid bodies using orthogonal transformations, Euler angles, and rotating reference frames, including the analysis of Coriolis and related (non) inertial effects. 513_PHY_F312.pdf.topics:
This is a first course on Statistical mechanics aimed at students who have familiarity with classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and classical thermodynamics. The stress is on developing the essential techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics for non-interacting systems. Classical Thermodynamics, as a study of macroscopic properties of materials, is no doubt an incredibly elegant interface between us and nature. Historically born out of the remarkable power of empiricism in the nineteenth century, the laws of Thermodynamics have stood the test of time. In its breadth of generality and profundity, the subject has found applications in almost all areas of fundamental and applied sciences. Here, we must note that scientific pedagogy is not necessarily chronologically ordered. The fast development in our understanding of matter at the microscopic level through advances in the atomic theories in the twentieth century required classical thermodynamics to find reconciliation with physics at the microscopic level. The role of statistics in bridging the laws of mechanics with those of thermodynamics is probably as profound as the laws themselves. In a first course on statistical mechanics aimed towards a target audience comprising undergraduate students of basic sciences and engineering it is important to reveal the subject in its broad, multi-layered beauty. The course aims to look at Thermodynamics as an emergent phenomenon and emphasize the role of statistics in bridging the microscopic and macroscopic descriptions.

❖ Develop familiarity with the basic techniques of equilibrium statistical mechanics. ❖ Understand the role of probability theory and statistics in relating microscopic and macroscopic descriptions of thermodynamic systems ❖ Learn key methods of ensemble theory ❖ Distinguish between quantum and classical statistical mechanics and compute essential properties of ideal Bosonic and Fermionic systems.

516_PHY_F413.pdf.topics:
(Just as every book has a preface, I will avail this space to elaborate about the course in great detail. It will be a synopsis of particle physics, providing context for the questions it addresses and a sense of the answers that will be discussed in the course. Hopefully, it will give you a fair idea of what particle physics is all about and what to expect from this course. The titles of paragraphs may seem out of place or even nonsensical in the first reading. Some things will fall in place as you read through the handout. For some other stuff, you may have to wait till the end of the course.) Bright blue sky: What are the most fundamental questions we can pose in Physics? 1. What are the most fundamental building blocks (called particles for the want of a better word) of the Universe? 2. What are the fundamental forces (interaction is a better word) that bind them to form the structural hierarchy we see at different levels? 3. What can we know about the particles and their dynamics if we know the answers to the above questions? 4. Are there fundamental principles that mandate the existence of different kinds of fundamental particles and different kinds of fundamental interactions? Is there an overarching theme in the answers we know? Particle Physics aims to offer concrete answers to the above questions, though some caveats remain. Our present understanding of these questions is summarised in the so-called Standard Model (SM) of Particle Physics. This course will offer some answers within the framework of the Standard Model of Particle Physics. Relativity + Quantum Mechanics = Quantum Field Theory: Before I give a glimpse of answers to the above questions, we must ask for the framework for particle physics. It turns out that the natural framework for particle physics is a quantum theory for a system of fields. Let us understand the reason behind this. We will be talking about the most fundamental particles and their interactions at the minutest length scales, so quantum mechanics is inescapable. To study smaller and smaller length scales, we need probes whose wavelengths are sufficiently small. Thus, we use extremely high-energy particles (relativistic velocities imply larger momentum and hence smaller wavelengths). Hence, special relativity is a must. How about the study of mesons (bound states of quarks-antiquarks) and 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division baryons (bound states of three quarks)? Here again, surprisingly, it is quantum mechanics that ensures relativistic conditions. Whenever you confine a quantum system to a tiny volume, uncertainties in the momenta become extremely large, implying relativistic conditions. Thus, quarks inside protons and neutrons are quite hot and hence relativistic. Now, under relativistic conditions, you can literally "cook" an arbitrarily large number of particles-antiparticle pairs, if you pump in a sufficient amount of energy. Thus, your underlying dynamical system must be inherently capable of describing situations involving an arbitrarily large number of particles. Thus, any framework with a fixed number of particles is doomed to fail. A system of fields with infinitely many degrees of freedom is the right dynamical system to describe relativistic interactions. Thus, relativity + quantum mechanics = Quantum Field Theory. Quantum Field Theory is demanding, and a typical graduate school has at least two courses in Quantum Field Theory before one can survey any literature in Particle Physics. However, the purpose of any undergraduate course in particle physics is essentially twofold: a) to provide a glimpse of the power of symmetry principles in the origin and classification of fundamental particles and their interactions, and b) to demonstrate the power of perturbative calculations of scattering cross-sections and decay rates via Feynman rules. To meet this end, we will follow an approach pioneered by Richard Feynman. This is the structure and approach of a first course in particle physics worldwide. It is just not possible to do squeeze in relativistic quantum field theory and particle physics in one semester, without any prior exposure to either of them. From relativistic quantum mechanics to scattering cross-sections and decay rate: Answers to questions 1 and 2 have been the content of the latter half of your Nuclear and Particle Physics course. The focus of this course would be essentially on questions 3 and 4. It turns out that we know a lot about the fundamental particles and their interactions. In the first module, we will primarily focus on calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates. To do this, we will quickly recap the special theory of relativity (module 1) and the time-dependent perturbation theory (module 2). In Module 2, we will also discuss the relativistic quantum mechanics of spin-0 particles (the Klein-Gordon equation). Module-3 will introduce spin-1/2 particles (Dirac equation) and apply them to classic scattering cross-section calculations in quantum electrodynamics at lowest order in perturbation theory. You will see the famous Feynman diagrams and Feynman rules in action.. We will have some fun with what one can do with the rules, and that is calculating scattering cross-sections and decay rates, which experimentalists can actually measure. Indiscreet fall of the discrete symmetries: Symmetry transformations can be continuous or discrete. Discrete symmetries are essentially invariances under a discrete transformation and will be the subject of module-4. Their examples are parity (P) (inversion about origin, i.e., changing x,y,z to -x,-y,-z), time reversal (T) (changing t to -t), and charge conjugation (C) (changing particles to antiparticles and vice versa). Naively, Physics was expected to be invariant under each of these discrete transformations separately. However, it turns out that individually, each of them is violated. In fact, the so-called CPT theorem states that any Lorentz-invariant local quantum field theory with a Hermitian Hamiltonian must be invariant under the combined transformation of Charge conjugation (C), Parity (P), and Time reversal (T). It turns out that the weak interactions violate all three (C, P, and T) and also the combination CP. However, the combined CPT transformation is so far known to be an exact symmetry and any violation of CPT would signal a fundamental trouble either in quantum mechanics or relativity or local interactions. The Story of the separate violations of C, P, and T is intricately tied to the story of weak interaction and will be covered in module 5. Building the Universe from scratch - the blocks and the glue: 2 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Module-6 would be the last module of the course and will answer question number 4 in the affirmative and offer a convincing discourse on the same. Until the advent of Particle Physics in the 20th century, symmetries and conservation laws largely served a utilitarian purpose of bookkeeping. Conservation laws offer our first shot at dynamics without having to confront the dynamics head-on. Just look at the stuff before and after a dynamical event, and if conservation laws are applicable, we can pull out the unknown energy or momentum by a straightforward bookkeeping of conserved quantum numbers. However, during the latter half of the 20th century, we learnt that the symmetries aren’t just utilitarian. They are the rhyme and the reason behind why things are the way they are. What do you need to build the Universe from scratch? The bricks (fundamental particles), the cement (glue to bind them to form bound states), and a blueprint (the Lagrangian). All of these and much more are a consequence of some symmetry principles which can be broadly divided into two categories -- spacetime symmetries (Lorentz or, strictly speaking, Poincaré symmetries), and internal or local gauge symmetries. So the question of kinematics, or why the fundamental particles of different mass and spin exist at all, is answered by the spacetime symmetries. Particles of different mass and spin exist as representations of Poincare group. On the other hand, the question of the existence of three different fundamental interactions (excluding gravity for the moment) is answered by the "internal" local gauge symmetries. They are "internal" in the sense that they operate in an abstract internal space different from the "external" spacetime. All the fundamental interactions are explained within the overarching theme of gauge theories. How to break a symmetry without actually breaking it? A massive question: If you think the question is an oxymoron and with a blatant misuse of adjectives, please bear with me until the mist clears. We now have the basic building blocks (particles) and the glue (interactions) which bind them in place as a consequence of spacetime (Poincaré) and internal (Gauge) symmetries. But what is the origin of the mass of the particles? It turns out that you cannot just put a mass term in your fundamental Lagrangian by hand and get on with the business. The question of mass is intricately tied to the question of Lorentz invariance and gauge invariance, and will be covered in the latter half of module 6. In a jigsaw puzzle, each piece is constrained by the shape of the neighbouring pieces. We cannot accommodate mass without fundamentally tweaking the particle content and introducing a "subtle breaking" of the gauge symmetries. There are three different ways in which a symmetry can be broken: explicit, spontaneous, and anomalous (beyond the scope of the course). It turns out that putting a mass term by hand explicitly breaks the local gauge symmetry, and that is nothing short of a sacrilege in particle physics. We can nevertheless break it through the "back door", that is, break it spontaneously! Our Lagrangian, equations of motion, commutation relations, and Feynman rules all respect gauge symmetry, and yet, the choice of a ground state violates the symmetry. Spontaneous symmetry breaking may appear mysterious, but it is rather common. The most famous example is that of a ferromagnet. Its Hamiltonian is invariant under rotational symmetry. This is why, above a critical temperature called the Curie temperature, thanks to thermal agitation, all the spin dipoles are randomly oriented and hence the net magnetization averages out to zero. However, below the Curie temperature, all dipoles spontaneously align in a specific direction, giving non-zero net magnetization. The Hamiltonian is still rotationally invariant, and yet magnetic dipoles select a specific direction and align. It turns out that to realize such spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics, we need to add a spin-0 field and its accompanying dynamics. How exactly the machinery of the Higgs mechanism and spontaneous symmetry breaking end up endowing fundamental particles with mass cannot be elaborated here. It is said that the proof of the pudding is in eating. We hope to get this far and discuss these issues. 3 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division Dark Clouds: We started with bright blue skies and end with dark clouds. I wish I could end this preface on a positive note. However, truth be told, all of our knowledge about fundamental particles and their interactions is like a small lamp in a largely dark room. I am collecting here a laundry list of questions about which we have only speculations to offer without any hint of empirical verification.

The above description conveys the scope and objective in great detail.

518_PHY_F422.pdf.topics:
This is an introductory course on Group Theory, designed for undergraduates and PhD scholars, with an emphasis on applications in physics. Many physical systems exhibit symmetry, which allows for a simplified analysis. The mathematical language of describing and studying a vast class of these symmetries is Group Theory. In each case, the symmetry operations are represented by individual group elements and their combinations. Discrete symmetries entail discrete groups, which may contain a finite or infinite number of elements. Continuous symmetries entail continuous groups (also called as ‘Lie groups’). In this course, we will cover the structure, classification, and representations of groups. We will see how group theory can help us understands some aspects of quantum mechanics, classical mechanics, and most importantly, particle interactions.

• Identify and classify discrete and continuous symmetries in physical systems using the foundational concepts of group theory. • Apply the principles of representation theory to decompose group representations into irreducible components and interpret their physical significance. • Demonstrate the application of group theory in quantum mechanics by analyzing the symmetry structure of the hydrogen atom and explaining the role of conserved quantities and degeneracies. • Analyze physical systems under spacetime symmetry transformations using continuous groups such as the Lorentz and Poincaré groups. • Analyze particle interactions and fundamental forces using the mathematical framework of Lie groups and Lie algebras.

522_PHY_U101.pdf.topics:
This course takes us from the study of oscillations to waves, and finally to the foundations of quantum mechanics, tracing a connected thread through classical and modern physics. We begin with an introduction to oscillations and the model of simple harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, leading to the phenomenon of resonance. We shall study coupled oscillators: normal modes and frequencies, and the continuum limit of a large number of coupled oscillators. We will study transverse vibrations of a stretched string, the one-dimensional wave equation, and traveling wave solutions to the wave equation. We shall study energy transport in waves and pulses on a string, and their interaction with a boundary: reflection and refraction. Wave phenomena, such as the interference of light waves from two coherent sources, will lead us to wave-particle duality, the concept of the photon, the de Broglie hypothesis, and matter waves. We shall study the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Schrödinger equation, and the wavefunction. We shall study the quantum problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box, energy quantization, barrier tunneling, the transmission coefficient, and introduce scanning tunneling microscopy as an application of quantum tunneling.

● Understand oscillatory motion: Analyze simple harmonic motion, superposition of oscillations, and the effects of damping and external driving forces, including resonance and quality factor ● Master the physics of coupled systems and waves: Explain how coupled oscillators lead to normal modes, and how taking the continuum limit gives rise to wave phenomena, including the wave equation, traveling waves, and energy transport ● Analyze wave behavior and propagation: Distinguish between group and phase velocity, and describe how waves interact with boundaries and each other through reflection, refraction, and interference ● Grasp the foundations of quantum mechanics: Explain wave-particle duality, the de Broglie hypothesis, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and apply the Schrödinger equation to determine wavefunctions and 1 BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani Pilani Campus AUGS/ AGSR Division energy quantization in simple systems ● Apply quantum tunneling to real-world technology: Calculate transmission coefficients for barrier tunneling and connect this phenomenon to practical applications such as scanning tunneling microscopy

Introduction to oscillations, simple harmonic motion, superposition of harmonic oscillations, damped and forced oscillations, resonance and quality factor: transverse and longitudinal waves, wave speed in a stretched string, wave equation in one dimension, traveling solutions to the wave equation, energy transport in waves, standing waves, travelling sound waves; Interference of light waves, introduction to diffraction; concept of photon, photoelectric effect, Compton scattering; wave-particle duality, de Broglie hypothesis and matter waves; 1D Quantum wave functions: properties and applications; Pauli’s exclusion principle and multielectrons atoms, introduction to X-rays and Lasers.

This course introduces the fundamental concepts of classical and quantum waves, beginning with simple harmonic motion as the basis of oscillatory phenomena and progressing through mechanical waves, sound, interference, and diffraction. It then explores the transition from classical to quantum physics by examining the wave-particle nature of light and matter, culminating in an elementary introduction to quantum wave functions and their applications to atomic systems, X-rays, and lasers. Designed for undergraduate students with a basic knowledge of calculus, the course emphasizes physical intuition, conceptual understanding, and qualitative reasoning over advanced mathematical formalism. Its objective is to provide a unified understanding of wave phenomena across classical and quantum physics, establish the conceptual foundations of modern physics, and prepare students for advanced courses in optics, quantum mechanics, condensed matter physics, and related disciplines.

Success in any organization—from the smallest corner store to the largest multinational corporation—requires the use of cost accounting concepts and practices. Cost accounting provides key data to managers for planning and controlling, as well as costing products, services, even customers. Cost accounting is one of very important managerial tool for business strategy and implementation.

This course focuses on how cost accounting helps managers make better decisions, as cost accountants are increasingly becoming integral members of their company’s decision-making teams. The objectives of the course are mentioned below: i. This course will equip students with the knowledge and analytical skills required to apply management accounting tools and techniques for planning, decision making, cost control, and performance evaluation in organizations.

533_SNS_F211.pdf.topics:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials, their synthesis and properties, with emphasis on their size-dependent physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanostructures. Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological domains. This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into advanced study or research in the field.

534_SNS_F214.pdf.topics:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to the fundamental concepts of solid-state physics with a particular emphasis on semiconductor materials and their applications. It covers crystal structures and defects, the quantum and statistical principles governing electron behavior in solids, the origin of energy bands, and the electronic properties of metals, semiconductors, and insulators. The course further introduces carrier transport mechanisms, including drift, diffusion, and the Hall effect, before discussing the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids. Throughout the course, the underlying physical principles are connected to modern semiconductor devices such as LEDs, solar cells, photodetectors, and sensors, providing students with the essential foundation required for advanced studies in materials science, condensed matter physics, and semiconductor technology.

This course introduces the fundamental principles of solid-state physics that underpin the behavior of crystalline materials and modern semiconductor devices. It encompasses crystal structures, basic quantum and statistical concepts, electronic band theory, semiconductor physics, and the thermal, magnetic, and optical properties of solids, while emphasizing their relevance to contemporary electronic and optoelectronic technologies. The primary objective is to develop a clear understanding of the relationship between the atomic structure of solids and their physical properties, explain the quantum mechanical origin of electronic behavior in materials, introduce the principles governing charge transport in semiconductors, and establish the scientific foundation necessary for the study, analysis, and application of semiconductor materials and devices in advanced engineering and physics courses.

535_SNS_F242.pdf.topics:
(as per the Bulletin): Crystal structure and growth of semiconductor, electrical conduction in solids, Elementary quantum physics (Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions, forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors (JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor devices. This course starts with explanation on crystal structure, semiconductor materials, fundamentals of semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic diodes will also be discussed in this course.

Softwareengineeringisadisciplinethatallowsustoapplyengineeringandcomputersciencecon- cepts in the development and maintenance of reliable, usable, and dependable software. 540_SW_E101.pdf.topics:
Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity & Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety.

This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core emotional, social and legal literacy for a healthy campus life. This includes conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior and building awareness against substance abuse.
